{{Short description|Mathematical term in group theory}}
In the [[Mathematics|mathematical]] area of [[group theory]], the '''Grigorchuk group''' or '''the first Grigorchuk group''' is a [[finitely generated group]] constructed by [[Rostislav Grigorchuk]] that provided the first example of a [[finitely generated group]] of intermediate (that is, faster than polynomial but slower than exponential) [[growth rate (group theory)|growth]]. The group was originally constructed by Grigorchuk in a 1980 paper<ref name="G0"/> and he then proved in a 1984 paper<ref name="G"/> that this group has intermediate growth, thus providing an answer to an important [[open problem]] posed by [[John Milnor]] in 1968. The Grigorchuk group remains a key object of study in [[geometric group theory]], particularly in the study of the so-called branch groups and automata groups, and it has important connections with the theory of [[iterated monodromy group]]s.<ref name="N">Volodymyr Nekrashevych. [https://books.google.com/books?id=QG9f1Dn_RlwC&q=Volodymyr+Nekrashevych.+%22Self-similar+groups%22 ''Self-similar groups.''] Mathematical Surveys and Monographs, 117. American Mathematical Society, Providence, RI, 2005. {{ISBN|0-8218-3831-8}}.</ref>

==History and significance==

The [[growth rate (group theory)|growth]] of a [[finitely generated group]] measures the asymptotics, as <math>n \to \infty</math> of the size of an ''n''-ball in the [[Cayley graph]] of the group (that is, the number of elements of ''G'' that can be expressed as words of length at most ''n'' in the generating set of ''G''). The study of growth rates of [[finitely generated group]]s goes back to the 1950s and is motivated in part by the notion of [[volume entropy]] (that is, the growth rate of the volume of balls) in the [[universal covering space]] of a [[compact space|compact]] [[Riemannian manifold]] in [[differential geometry]]. It is obvious that the growth rate of a finitely generated group is at most [[exponential function|exponential]] and it was also understood early on that finitely generated [[nilpotent group]]s have polynomial growth. In 1968 [[John Milnor]] posed a question<ref>John Milnor, Problem No. 5603, [[American Mathematical Monthly]], vol. 75 (1968), pp. 685&ndash;686.</ref> about the existence of a finitely generated group of ''intermediate growth'', that is, faster than any polynomial function and slower than any exponential function. An important result in the subject is [[Gromov's theorem on groups of polynomial growth]], obtained by [[Mikhail Gromov (mathematician)|Gromov]] in 1981, which shows that a finitely generated group has polynomial growth [[if and only if]] this group has a [[nilpotent group|nilpotent]] [[subgroup]] of finite [[index of a subgroup|index]]. Prior to Grigorchuk's work, there were many results establishing growth dichotomy (that is, that the growth is always either polynomial or exponential) for various classes of finitely generated groups, such as [[linear group]]s, [[solvable group]]s,<ref>[[John Milnor]]. [http://intlpress.com/JDG/archive/pdf/1968/2-4-447.pdf ''Growth of finitely generated solvable groups.''] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110523202053/http://intlpress.com/JDG/archive/pdf/1968/2-4-447.pdf |date=2011-05-23 }} [[Journal of Differential Geometry]]. vol. 2 (1968), pp. 447&ndash;449.</ref><ref>Joseph Rosenblatt. ''Invariant Measures and Growth Conditions'', [[Transactions of the American Mathematical Society]], vol. 193 (1974), pp. 33&ndash;53.</ref> etc.

Grigorchuk's group ''G'' was constructed in a 1980 paper of [[Rostislav Grigorchuk]],<ref name="G0">R. I. Grigorchuk. ''On Burnside's problem on periodic groups.'' (Russian) Funktsionalyi Analiz i ego Prilozheniya, vol. 14 (1980), no. 1, pp. 53&ndash;54.</ref> where he proved that this group is infinite, [[periodic group|periodic]] and [[residually finite group|residually finite]]. In a subsequent 1984 paper<ref name="G">R. I. Grigorchuk, ''Degrees of growth of finitely generated groups and the theory of invariant means.'' Izvestiya Akademii Nauk SSSR. Seriya Matematicheskaya. vol. 48 (1984), no. 5, pp. 939&ndash;985.</ref> Grigorchuk proved that this group has intermediate growth (this result was announced by Grigorchuk in 1983).<ref>{{cite journal| last=Grigorchuk | first=R. I. | year=1983 | script-title=ru:К проблеме Милнора о групповом росте |trans-title=On the Milnor problem of group growth | language=Russian | journal=[[Doklady Akademii Nauk SSSR]] | volume=271 | issue=1 | pages=30–33}}</ref> More precisely, he proved that ''G'' has growth ''b''(''n'') that is faster than <math>\exp(\sqrt n)</math> but slower than <math>\exp(n^s)</math> where <math>s=\log_{32}31\approx 0.991</math>. The upper bound was later improved by [[Laurent Bartholdi]]<ref>Laurent Bartholdi. ''Lower bounds on the growth of a group acting on the binary rooted tree.'' International Journal of Algebra and Computation, vol. 11 (2001), no. 1, pp. 73&ndash;88.</ref> to

:<math>s=\frac{\log2}{\log2-\log\eta} \approx 0.7674, \qquad \eta^3+\eta^2+\eta=2.</math>

A lower bound of <math>\exp(n^{0.504})</math> was proved by [[Yurii Leonov]].<ref>Yu. G. Leonov, ''On a lower bound for the growth of a 3-generator 2-group.'' Matematicheskii Sbornik, vol. 192 (2001), no. 11, pp. 77&ndash;92; translation in: Sbornik Mathematics. vol. 192 (2001), no. 11&ndash;12, pp. 1661&ndash;1676.</ref> It was conjectured that the limit

:<math>\lim_{n\to \infty} \log_n \log b(n),</math>

and this remained a major open problem until the problem was resolved in 2020 by [[Anna Erschler]] and [[Tianyi Zheng]]<ref>
[[Anna Erschler]], [[Tianyi Zheng]] "Growth of periodic Grigorchuk groups." [[Inventiones Mathematicae]], vol. 219 (2020), no.3,
pp 1069&ndash;1155.</ref> in which it was shown that the limit equals <math>s</math>.

Grigorchuk's group was also the first example of a group that is [[amenable group|amenable]] but not [[elementary amenable group|elementary amenable]], thus answering a problem posed by [[Mahlon Marsh Day]] in 1957.<ref>Mahlon M. Day. ''Amenable semigroups.'' Illinois Journal of Mathematics, vol. 1 (1957), pp. 509&ndash;544.</ref>

Originally, Grigorchuk's group ''G'' was constructed as a group of Lebesgue-measure-preserving transformations on the unit interval, but subsequently simpler descriptions of ''G'' were found and it is now usually presented as a group of automorphisms of the infinite regular [[binary tree|binary]] [[rooted tree]]. The study of Grigorchuk's group informed in large part the development of the theory of branch groups, automata groups and self-similar groups in the 1990s&ndash;2000s and Grigorchuk's group remains a central object in this theory. Recently important connections between this theory and [[complex dynamics]], particularly the notion of [[iterated monodromy group]]s, have been uncovered in the work of [[Volodymyr Nekrashevych]],<ref>Volodymyr Nekrashevych, [https://books.google.com/books?id=QG9f1Dn_RlwC&q=Volodymyr+Nekrashevych.+%22Self-similar+groups%22 ''Self-similar groups.''] Mathematical Surveys and Monographs, 117. American Mathematical Society, Providence, RI, 2005. {{ISBN|0-8218-3831-8}}.</ref> and others.

After Grigorchuk's 1984 paper, there were many subsequent extensions and generalizations.<ref>Roman Muchnik, and [[Igor Pak]]. ''On growth of Grigorchuk groups.'' International Journal of Algebra and Computation, vol. 11 (2001), no. 1, pp. 1&ndash;17.</ref><ref>Laurent Bartholdi. {{Deprecated archive|url=https://archive.today/20120710140134/http://imrn.oxfordjournals.org/cgi/reprint/1998/20/1049|title=''The growth of Grigorchuk's torsion group.''}} International Mathematics Research Notices, 1998, no. 20, pp. 1049&ndash;1054.</ref><ref>[[Anna Erschler]]. [http://aif.cedram.org/fitem?id=AIF_2005__55_2_493_0 ''Critical constants for recurrence of random walks on G-spaces.''] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110725151840/http://aif.cedram.org/fitem?id=AIF_2005__55_2_493_0 |date=2011-07-25 }} Université de Grenoble. Annales de l'Institut Fourier, vol. 55 (2005), no. 2, pp. 493&ndash;509.</ref><ref>Jeremie Brieussel, [http://www.institut.math.jussieu.fr/theses/2008/brieussel/ Growth of certain groups] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111002003942/http://www.institut.math.jussieu.fr/theses/2008/brieussel/ |date=2011-10-02 }},  Doctoral Dissertation, University of Paris, 2008.</ref>

==Definition==
[[File:T2 tree.svg|thumb|200px|The infinite binary tree {{math|''T''<sub>2</sub>}}. Its nodes are labeled by strings of 0s and 1s.]]
Although initially the Grigorchuk group was defined as a group of [[Lebesgue measure]]-preserving transformations of the unit interval, at present this group is usually given by its realization as a group of automorphisms of the infinite regular [[binary tree|binary]] [[rooted tree]]&nbsp;{{math|''T''<sub>2</sub>}}.  The tree {{math|''T''<sub>2</sub>}} is the set {{math|&Sigma;<sup>*</sup>}} of all finite strings in the alphabet&nbsp;{{math|&Sigma; {{=}} {{mset|0,1}}}}, including the [[empty string]]&nbsp;{{math|&emptyset;}}, which roots {{math|''T''<sub>2</sub>}}. For a vertex&nbsp;{{mvar|x}} of {{math|''T''<sub>2</sub>}} the string {{math|''x''0}} is the [[Binary tree|left child]] of {{mvar|x}} and the string {{math|''x''1}} is the [[Binary tree|right child]] of {{mvar|x}} in {{math|''T''<sub>2</sub>}}. The group of all automorphisms&nbsp;{{math|Aut(''T''<sub>2</sub>)}} can thus be thought of as the group of all length-preserving [[permutation group|permutations]]&nbsp;{{math|σ}} of {{math|&Sigma;<sup>*</sup>}} that also respect the ''initial segment'' relation: whenever a string&nbsp;{{mvar|x}} is an initial segment of a string&nbsp;{{mvar|y}} then {{math|σ(''x'')}} is an initial segment of {{math|σ(''y'')}}.

The '''Grigorchuk group'''&nbsp;{{mvar|G}} is the [[subgroup]] of {{math|Aut(''T''<sub>2</sub>)}} [[Generating set of a group|generated]] by four specific elements of {{math|Aut(''T''<sub>2</sub>)}} defined as follows (note that {{math|&emptyset;}} is [[fixpoint|fixed]] by ''any'' tree-automorphism): <math display=block>G = \langle a, b, c, d \rangle \leq \text{Aut}(T_2)\text{,}</math> where <math display=block>a(0) = 1\text{,} \qquad a(1) = 0\text{,} \qquad \forall x \in \Sigma^*\quad \begin{cases} a(0x) = 1x \\ a(1x) =0x \end{cases}</math> and <math display=block>
\begin{align}
&b(0) = c(0) = d(0) = 0 \\
&b(1) = c(1) = d(1) = 1\text{,} 
\end{align} \qquad \forall x \in \Sigma^*\quad  \begin{align} &\begin{cases} b(0x) = 0a(x) \\ b(1x) = 1c(x) \end{cases}  \\ &\begin{cases} c(0x) = 0a(x) \\ c(1x) = 1d(x) \end{cases} \\ &\begin{cases} d(0x) = 0x \\ d(1x) = 1b(x)\text{.}\end{cases} \end{align}
</math>

[[File:Grigorchuk group generators.svg|400px|thumb|The action of the standard generating set of the Grigorchuk group on the tree ''T''<sub>2</sub>. The triangles denote infinite subtrees that remain unchanged.]]

Only the element {{mvar|a}} is defined explicitly; it swaps the child trees of {{math|&emptyset;}}.  The elements {{mvar|b}}, {{mvar|c}}, and {{mvar|d}} are defined through a [[mutual recursion]].  

To understand the effect of the latter operations, consider the rightmost branch&nbsp;{{mvar|B}} of {{math|''T''<sub>2</sub>}}, which begins {{math|{{mset|&emptyset;, 1, 11, 111, ...}}}}.  As a branch, {{mvar|B}} is [[order-isomorphic]] to <math>\mathbb{N}.</math>  The original tree {{math|''T''<sub>2</sub>}} can be obtained by rooting a tree isomorphic to {{math|''T''<sub>2</sub>}} at each element of {{mvar|B}}; conversely, one can decompose {{math|''T''<sub>2</sub>}} into isomorphic subtrees indexed by elements of <math>B \cong  \mathbb{N}</math>.

The operations {{mvar|b}}, {{mvar|c}}, and {{mvar|d}} all respect this decomposition: they fix each element of {{mvar|B}} and act as automorphisms on each indexed subtree.  When {{mvar|b}} acts, it fixes every subtree with index {{math|&equiv; 2 (mod 3)}}, but acts as {{mvar|a}} on the rest.  Likewise, when {{mvar|c}} acts, it fixes only the subtrees of index {{math|&equiv; 1 (mod 3)}}; and {{mvar|d}} fixes those of index {{math|&equiv; 0 (mod 3)}}.  

A compact notation for these operations is as follows: let the left (resp. right) branch of {{math|''T''<sub>2</sub>}} be {{math|''T<sub>L</sub>'' {{=}} 0&Sigma;<sup>*</sup>}} (resp. {{math|''T<sub>R</sub>'' {{=}} 1&Sigma;<sup>*</sup>}}), so that <math display=block> a(T_L) \subseteq T_R, \quad a(T_R) \subseteq T_L\text{.}</math>  We write {{math|''f'' {{=}} (''g'', ''h'')}} to mean that {{mvar|f}} acts as {{mvar|g}} on {{math|''T<sub>L</sub>''}} and as {{mvar|h}} on {{math|''T<sub>R</sub>''}}.  Thus <math display=block> \begin{align}
b =(a,c) \quad &\Longleftrightarrow \quad  b(x) = \begin{cases} a(x) & x \in T_L \\ c(x) & x \in T_R \end{cases} \\
c =(a,d) \quad &\Longleftrightarrow \quad  c(x) = \begin{cases} a(x) & x \in T_L \\ d(x) & x \in T_R \end{cases} \\
d =(\text{id},b) \quad &\Longleftrightarrow \quad  d(x) = \begin{cases} x & x \in T_L \\ b(x) & x \in T_R\text{.} \end{cases} 
\end{align}</math>  Similarly <math display=block> aba = (c, a), \quad aca = (d, a), \quad ada = (b, \text{id})\text{,}</math> where {{math|id}} is the [[identity function]].

==Properties==

The following are basic algebraic properties of the Grigorchuk group (see<ref name="DH">Pierre de la Harpe. [https://books.google.com/books?id=60fTzwfqeQIC&dq=de+la+Harpe.+Topics+in+geometric+group+theory&pg=PP1 ''Topics in geometric group theory.''] Chicago Lectures in Mathematics. University of Chicago Press, Chicago. {{ISBN|0-226-31719-6}}; Ch. VIII, The first Grigorchuk group, pp. 211&ndash;264.</ref> for proofs):

*The group <math>G</math> is infinite.<ref name="G"/>
*The group <math>G</math> is [[residually finite group|residually finite]].<ref name="G"/> Let <math>\rho_n : G \to \text{Aut}(T[n])</math> be the restriction homomorphism that sends every element of <math>G</math> to its restriction to the first {{mvar|n}} levels of {{math|''T''<sub>2</sub>}}. The groups Aut(''T''[''n'']) are finite and for every nontrivial ''g'' in <math>G</math> there exists ''n'' such that <math>\rho_n (g) \neq 1.</math>
*The group <math>G</math> is generated by ''a'' and any two of the three elements ''b,c,d''. For example, we can write <math>G = \langle a, b, c\rangle.</math>
*The elements ''a'', ''b'', ''c'', ''d'' are [[Involution (mathematics)#Group theory|involutions]].
*The elements ''b'', ''c'', ''d'' pairwise commute and ''bc'' = ''cb'' = ''d'', ''bd'' = ''db'' = ''c'', ''dc'' = ''cd'' = ''b'', so that <math>\langle b, c, d \rangle \leqslant G</math> is an [[abelian group]] of order 4 [[group isomorphism|isomorphic]] to the [[direct product of groups|direct product]] of two [[cyclic group]]s of order 2.
*Combining the previous two properties we see that every element of <math>G</math> can be written as a (positive) word in ''a'', ''b'', ''c'', ''d'' such that this word does not contain any subwords of the form ''aa'', ''bb'', ''cc'', ''dd'', ''cd'', ''dc'', ''bc'', ''cb'', ''bd'', ''db''. Such words are called ''reduced''.
*The group <math>G</math> is a [[p-group|2-group]], that is, every element in ''G'' has finite [[Order (group theory)|order]] that is a power of 2.<ref name="G0"/>
*The group <math>G</math> is periodic (as a 2-group) and not locally finite (as it is finitely generated). As such, it is a counterexample to the [[Burnside problem]].
*The group <math>G</math> has intermediate growth.<ref name="G"/>
*The group <math>G</math> is [[amenable group|amenable]] but not [[elementary amenable group|elementary amenable]].<ref name="G"/>
*The group <math>G</math> is ''[[just infinite group|just infinite]]'', that is ''G'' is infinite but every proper [[quotient group]] of ''G'' is finite.
*The group <math>G</math> has the ''congruence subgroup property'': a subgroup ''H'' has finite [[index of a subgroup|index]] in <math>G</math> if and only if there is a positive integer ''n'' such that <math>\ker(\rho_n) \leqslant H.</math>
*The group <math>G</math> has solvable [[subgroup membership problem]], that is, there is an algorithm that, given arbitrary words ''w'', ''u''<sub>1</sub>, ..., ''u<sub>n</sub>'' decides whether or not ''w''  represents an element of the subgroup generated by ''u''<sub>1</sub>, ..., ''u<sub>n</sub>''.<ref name="GW"/>
*The group <math>G</math> is [[LERF|subgroup separable]], that is, every finitely generated subgroup is closed in the [[Profinite group|pro-finite topology]] on <math>G</math>.<ref name="GW">R. I.Grigorchuk, and J. S. Wilson. [http://journals.cambridge.org/action/displayAbstract;jsessionid=61D43BDA6A49AF3EA6074EE64ADB3071.tomcat1?fromPage=online&aid=186399 ''A structural property concerning abstract commensurability of subgroups.''] [[Journal of the London Mathematical Society]] (2), vol. 68 (2003), no. 3, pp. 671&ndash;682.</ref>
*Every [[maximal subgroup]] of <math>G</math> has finite [[index of a subgroup|index]] in <math>G</math>.<ref>E. L. Pervova, ''Everywhere dense subgroups of a group of tree automorphisms.'' (in Russian). Trudy Matematicheskogo Instituta Imeni V. A. Steklova. vol. 231 (2000), Din. Sist., Avtom. i Beskon. Gruppy, pp. 356&ndash;367; translation in: Proceedings of the Steklov Institute of Mathematics, vol 231 (2000), no. 4, pp. 339&ndash;350.</ref>
*The group <math>G</math> is finitely generated but not [[finitely presented group|finitely presentable]].<ref name="G"/><ref>I. G. Lysënok, ''A set of defining relations for the Grigorchuk group.'' Matematicheskie Zametki, vol. 38 (1985), no. 4, pp. 503&ndash;516.</ref>
*The [[Group action (mathematics)|stabilizer]] of the level one vertices in <math>T_2</math> in <math>G</math> (the subgroup of elements that act as identity on the strings 0 and 1), is generated by the following elements:
::<math>G_{\{0, 1\}} = \langle b, c, d, aba, aca, ada \rangle.</math>
:<math>G_{\{0, 1\}}</math> is a [[normal subgroup]] of [[index of a subgroup|index]] 2 in ''G'' and 
::<math> G = G_{\{0, 1\}} \sqcup a G_{\{0, 1\}}.</math>
*A reduced word represents an element of <math>G_{\{0, 1\}}</math>if and only if this word involves an even number of occurrences of ''a''.
*If ''w'' is a reduced word in ''G'' with a positive even number of occurrences of ''a'', then there exist words ''u'', ''v'' (not necessarily reduced) such that:
::<math> w = (u,v) \quad \text{and} \quad \begin{cases} |u|, |v| \leqslant \tfrac{1}{2} |w| & |w| \text{ odd} \\  |u|, |v| \leqslant \tfrac{1}{2} (|w|+1) & |w| \text{ even} \end{cases}</math>
:This is sometimes called the ''contraction property''. It plays a key role in many proofs regarding ''G'' since it allows to use inductive arguments on the length of a word.
*The group ''G'' has solvable [[Word problem for groups|word problem]] and solvable [[conjugacy problem]] (consequence of the contraction property).
